lines: An AI agent just changed production. And now, payments are down.
This is Trustfall. The command center for investigating what your AI agents did.
Meet the incident. The Payments A P I has failed.
I select the building, and the investigation opens.
OpsBot seven, an AI agent, was asked to tune staging. But at nine fourteen, it wrote a pool size of zero into production.
Twenty six seconds later, payments went dark.
Here is what makes Trustfall different. Two separate verdicts.
Identity: verified. Action: not authorized.
Knowing who acted is not the same as knowing it was allowed.
In the evidence graph, I select the change, and everything connected to it lights up. The agent, the policy it broke, and the outage.
Solid cyan lines are facts. Dashed amber lines are hypotheses.
Now, can we trust the evidence? Every record is signed, and verified live, right here.
Six records verify. The approval ticket is missing, and that is a finding too.
Tamper with a single record, and verification fails instantly.
But a valid signature proves integrity. Never authorization.
The A I investigator explains what happened, but it may only cite evidence that exists.
Every finding carries its evidence I D. The cause of the outage is marked as a hypothesis, because no record proves it.
And it tells you what is still unresolved. In this demo, it runs in deterministic fallback mode, with no live model.
Now, recovery. Isolate the agent, keep investigating, or restore the previous configuration.
I restore the verified snapshot. This recovery is simulated.
Watch the city heal. The network calms, and the incident resolves.
And the incident report writes itself, from live state. Ready to export as Markdown, or J S O N.
Trustfall. Trust the evidence. Not the signature alone.
